title: The M-/Wa- Noun Class and Subject Prefixes
subtitle: Human nouns and their mandatory verbal agreements
keyPoint: Nouns denoting human beings take the prefix m- in the singular and wa- in the plural, governing the verbal subject prefixes a- and wa-.

mistakes.note: A singular noun in the M-/Wa- class must take the singular subject concord 'a-', never plural 'wa-'.
Plural M-/Wa- nouns like wanafunzi require the matching plural agreement prefix 'wa-' on the verb.
First person singular 'mimi' triggers the subject prefix 'ni-', not third person 'a-'.

quiz.question: The teacher is speaking. -> 'Mwalimu ___sema.'
quiz.explanation: A singular human noun requires the third-person singular prefix 'a-', forming 'anasema'.

quiz.question: The children are playing. -> 'Watoto ___cheza.'
quiz.explanation: Plural human nouns take 'wa-' subject agreement combined with tense prefix '-na-', yielding 'wanacheza'.

quiz.question: Choose the correct plural form of 'Mgeni anafika.'
quiz.explanation: 'Mgeni' pluralizes to 'wageni' and its verb prefix shifts from 'a-' to 'wa-', giving 'Wageni wanafika.'

quiz.question: You (singular) are reading. -> 'Wewe ___soma.'
quiz.explanation: Second person singular pronoun 'wewe' takes the subject concord 'u-', resulting in 'unasoma'.

tip: Always remember: every human being belongs syntactically to the M-/Wa- class, so regardless of biological irregularities, the verb takes 'a-' in the singular and 'wa-' in the plural.

title: Present Continuous and Habitual Tense Prefix -na-
subtitle: Building verbs for current and ongoing actions
keyPoint: The infix -na- slots directly between the subject prefix and the verb root to indicate ongoing present actions.

useCases.label: Habitual Realities
useCases.example: Juma anafanya kazi katika benki kubwa.

examples.en: Yeye anasoma barua kutoka kwa rafiki.

mistakes.note: Swahili requires an explicit tense prefix; you cannot attach the subject marker directly to the root for present actions.
The infix '-na-' represents present time; past events require the past tense marker '-li-'.
Do not omit the subject marker 'a-'; '-na-' alone cannot carry personhood on standard verbs.

quiz.question: We are drinking water right now. -> 'Sisi ___kunywa maji.'
quiz.explanation: The blank precedes 'kunywa', so the subject concord 'tu-' plus present marker '-na-' gives 'tuna'.

quiz.question: I am studying today. -> 'Mimi ___ Kiswahili leo.'
quiz.explanation: First-person singular uses 'ni-' followed by present tense '-na-' and the stem '-soma': 'ninasoma'.

quiz.question: Which sentence correctly expresses 'They are arriving'?
quiz.explanation: 'Wao' (they) takes 'wa-' plus present tense '-na-' plus '-fika', yielding 'Wanafika sasa.'

quiz.question: You (plural) are listening. -> 'Ninyi ___sikiliza.'
quiz.explanation: The second person plural concord is 'm-' (before consonants) / 'mu-', combined with '-na-' to produce 'mnasikiliza'.

tip: Monosyllabic verbs (like kula 'eat' and kunywa 'drink') keep their infinitive prefix 'ku-' in the present affirmative: ninakula, not *ninala!

title: Present Tense Negation with ha-...-i
subtitle: Forming negative verbs in the present tense
keyPoint: To negate the present tense, apply negative subject prefixes, drop the tense marker -na-, and change the final verb vowel from -a to -i.

examples.en: Mimi sitaki chai ya moto sasa.

mistakes.note: Negation drops '-na-' entirely; for 'mimi', the fused prefix is 'si-', and final '-a' becomes '-i'.
Bantu-origin verbs ending in '-a' must shift their final vowel to '-i' in present negation (lala -> lali).
Verbs borrowed from Arabic (like jaribu, fahamu) do not shift their final vowel to '-i', but native ones do.

quiz.question: I do not want. -> 'Mimi ___.'
quiz.explanation: First person negative replaces 'ni-' with 'si-', drops '-na-', and changes '-taka' to '-taki'.

quiz.question: He does not speak Swahili. -> 'Yeye ___ Kiswahili.'
quiz.explanation: Third person singular negative prefix is 'ha-' paired with the modified verb stem 'semi'.

quiz.question: They do not know. -> 'Wao ___.'
quiz.explanation: 'Wao' negates with 'hawa-' + 'jui' (from '-jua' with final vowel shifting to '-i').

quiz.question: What is the negative present form of 'Wewe unafika'?
quiz.explanation: 'Wewe' negates with 'hu-', tense prefix '-na-' drops, and '-fika' becomes '-fiki'.

tip: Verbs borrowed from Arabic (ending in -e, -i, or -u, such as 'kusamehe', 'kufikiri', 'kujibu') retain their endings in the negative: 'sisamehe', 'sifikiri', 'sijibu'.

title: Past (-li-) and Future (-ta-) Tenses and Their Negation
subtitle: Talking about yesterday and tomorrow with -li-, -ta-, and negative -ku-
keyPoint: Past tense uses -li- (negated with -ku-) while future tense uses -ta- (negated with ha-...-ta- without changing the verb's final vowel).

useCases.label: Future Commitments
useCases.example: Kesho tutasafiri kwenda mji wa Arusha.

examples.en: Mimi niliona nyota angani jana usiku.
Sisi hatukuona simba katika mbuga ile.
Wewe hutakula chakula chote kile peke yako.
Asha alimaliza kazi yake mapema jana.

mistakes.note: In past negation with '-ku-', the final vowel remains '-a'; do not change it to '-i'.
Future negation retains the normal final '-a' of the verb root: 'sitasoma', not 'sitasomi'.
This spelling is standard, but watch out for confusing past negative 'haku-' with present negative 'ha-'.

quiz.question: Yesterday she arrived. -> 'Jana yeye ___.'
quiz.explanation: Past affirmative for 'yeye' requires subject marker 'a-' and past marker '-li-': 'alifika'.

quiz.question: We did not go yesterday. -> 'Sisi ___ jana.'
quiz.explanation: Past negation for 'sisi' combines negative prefix 'hatu-' with past negative marker '-ku-': 'hatukuenda'.

quiz.question: Tomorrow they will dance. -> 'Kesho wao ___.'
quiz.explanation: Future tense for 'wao' requires prefix 'wa-' with future marker '-ta-': 'watacheza'.

quiz.question: I will not drink coffee. -> 'Mimi ___ kahawa.'
quiz.explanation: Future negative combines 1st person 'si-' + '-ta-' + verb root (monosyllabic retains 'ku-'): 'sitakunywa'.

tip: Unlike present negation which forces '-a' to turn into '-i', both past negative (-ku-) and future negative (-ta-) KEEP the verb's final -a!

title: Possessive Concords with -a (The Associative Particle)
subtitle: Expressing 'my', 'your', 'his/her', and 'of' across noun classes
keyPoint: Possessive stems (-angu, -ako, -ake) and the preposition 'of' (-a) prefix agreement markers that strictly match the class of the possessed noun.

useCases.label: Associative 'Of' Relationships
useCases.example: Hiki ni kitabu cha mwalimu mkuu.

examples.en: Kitabu changu kiko juu ya meza.
Nyumba yetu ina madirisha makubwa mawili.
Gari la baba lina rangi nyeusi.

mistakes.note: 'Kitabu' belongs to the Ki-/Vi- class (Class 7), so the possessive concord must be 'ch-' (changu), not human 'wangu'.
'Mtoto' belongs to the M-/Wa- human class; the associative particle 'of' must take 'w-', becoming 'wa', not 'la'.
'Gari' belongs to the Ji-/Ma- noun class (Class 5), whose associative concord is 'l-', making 'la baba'.

quiz.question: My child is resting. -> 'Mtoto ___ anapumzika.'
quiz.explanation: 'Mtoto' is a Class 1 (human) noun, requiring the agreement consonant 'w-', yielding 'wangu'.

quiz.question: The book of the student. -> 'Kitabu ___ mwanafunzi.'
quiz.explanation: 'Kitabu' belongs to Class 7 (Ki- class), which takes the associative particle 'cha' (ki + a -> cha).

quiz.question: Our house is large. -> 'Nyumba ___ ni kubwa.'
quiz.explanation: 'Nyumba' (Class 9 N-class) takes the possessive concord 'y-', making 'yetu' (our house).

quiz.question: His friend arrived. -> 'Rafiki ___ alifika.'
quiz.explanation: Even though 'rafiki' takes loanword noun patterns, all animate persons take Class 1 agreement 'wake'.

tip: Possessives always follow the noun they describe in Swahili: say 'kitabu changu' (literally 'book my'), never *changu kitabu!

title: Locative Suffix -ni and Spatial Demonstratives
subtitle: Turn ordinary nouns into locations and navigate space with precise demonstratives
keyPoint: Appending the suffix -ni turns a standard noun into a location, while demonstratives distinguish specific (hapa), general (huku), and interior (humu) spatial dimensions.

mistakes.note: Proper nouns of places like cities and countries never take the suffix -ni.
Do not use 'kwa' for inanimate locations; attach the locative clitic -ni to the noun instead.
Use 'humu' directly to denote inside/interior location rather than mixing standard demonstratives with adverbs.

quiz.question: How do you say 'at home' in Swahili?
quiz.explanation: Adding -ni to 'nyumba' transforms the noun into the locative form 'nyumbani'.

quiz.question: Select the correct demonstrative for 'inside this room': 'Chumbani ___.'
quiz.explanation: 'Humu' is the Class 18 demonstrative denoting interior or contained space ('inside').

quiz.question: Which sentence correctly says 'I am going to Arusha'?
quiz.explanation: Proper city names do not receive the locative suffix -ni.

quiz.question: Choose the demonstrative denoting an exact, definite spot nearby: 'Keti ___.'
quiz.explanation: 'Hapa' indicates a specific, definite proximal point (Class 16).

tip: Never attach -ni to proper place names like Dar es Salaam, Mombasa, or Kenya.

title: Inanimate Noun Classes (Ki-/Vi- and M-/Mi-)
subtitle: Master concord prefixes for concrete objects, tools, plants, and trees
keyPoint: Inanimate nouns dictate all adjectives, verbs, and pronouns in a sentence through strict class concords: ki-/vi- for Class 7/8 and m-/mi- (verb u-/i-) for Class 3/4.

examples.en: Mlima ule mrefu una theluji nyingi.

mistakes.wrong: Mti mmoja uliangua, mti ule ulikuwa mkubwa sana.
mistakes.right: Mti mmoja ulianguka, mti ule ulikuwa mkubwa sana.
mistakes.note: Remember Class 3 takes the subject prefix 'u-', never 'a-' (which is reserved exclusively for people and animals in Class 1).
Possessives must agree with Class 7: 'changu', not the Class 9 form 'yangu'.
Class 4 plural nouns require the verbal subject prefix 'i-', not the Class 10 prefix 'zi-'.

quiz.question: Complete the agreement: 'Kisu kikali ___ nyama.' (The sharp knife cuts meat)
quiz.explanation: Class 7 nouns take the verbal subject prefix 'ki-', resulting in 'kinakata' in the present tense.

quiz.question: Which sentence exhibits correct Class 4 concord?
quiz.explanation: Class 4 takes adjective prefix 'mi-' (mizuri) and verbal prefix 'i-' (imenunuliwa).

quiz.question: Choose the correct plural form of 'Chombo kile kimevunjika':
quiz.explanation: 'Chombo' pluralizes to 'vyombo', and 'kile' pluralizes to 'vile' in Class 8.

quiz.question: Complete the sentence: 'Mti huu ___ matunda mengi.' (This tree has many fruits)
quiz.explanation: The subject concord for singular Class 3 nouns with the verb of association (-na) is 'u-', giving 'una'.

tip: Even though Class 3 nouns start with 'm-' like Class 1 humans, their subject prefix on verbs is 'u-' (plural 'i-'), never 'a-' or 'wa-'.

title: Object Infixes and Pronominal Incorporation
subtitle: Embed pronouns and direct objects directly inside the Swahili verb
keyPoint: Object infixes sit immediately preceding the verb root, and they are grammatically compulsory whenever referring to definite animate beings.

useCases.label: Pronominal substitution (replacing noun)
useCases.example: Je, unakiona kitabu change? Ndiyo, ninakiona.

mistakes.note: When the direct object is a specific human or animal, the object infix (-m-/-mw-) is mandatory.
Use the second-person singular object infix '-ku-' when addressing 'you', not '-mw-'.
Monosyllabic verbs like 'kula' drop the infinitive 'ku-' when taking an object infix: 'ali-ki-la'.

quiz.question: Insert the missing infix for 'I see you (singular)': 'Nina___ona.'
quiz.explanation: The 2nd person singular object infix is '-ku-' (ninakuona).

quiz.question: Select the sentence where the object infix correctly refers to 'vitabu' (books):
quiz.explanation: The object concord for Class 8 (vitabu) is '-vi-', producing 'ninavisoma'.

quiz.question: Which verb contains the 1st person plural ('us') object infix?
quiz.explanation: '-tu-' is the 1st person plural object infix: 'a-na-tu-penda' (he/she loves us).

quiz.question: Why is 'Nilimwona Juma' preferred over 'Niliona Juma'?
options: It is in the past tense.
Specific human objects require an object concord.
quiz.explanation: In Swahili, named or definite animate objects require an incorporated object infix.

tip: Position rule: Subject Prefix + Tense Marker + [OBJECT INFIX] + Verb Root. The object infix always clings directly to the root!

title: The Perfect Tense -me- vs State Verbs
subtitle: Differentiate completed actions, present resultant states, and the negative -ja-
keyPoint: The tense marker -me- denotes completed actions with current relevance or present bodily/mental states, while its negative counterpart replaces both subject prefix and tense with negative prefix + -ja-.

cells: he has arrived / not yet arrived
he is standing / not yet standing
we are seated / we haven't sat down
they have realized / don't yet know

examples.en: Nimeshiba sana baada ya chakula kile.
Sijala chochote tangu asubuhi ya leo.

mistakes.wrong: Ninasimama sasa (meaning: I am currently standing on my feet).
mistakes.note: Use '-me-' for stative verbs like 'kusimama' (to stand up) or 'kukaa' (to sit down) to describe the ongoing state of being seated/standing.
To convey 'has not yet done something', use the '-ja-' tense marker instead of the past negative '-ku-'.
Monosyllabic verbs lose their infinitive 'ku-' prefix in the negative perfect with '-ja-'.

quiz.question: How do you say 'They are seated / sitting down'?
quiz.explanation: 'Kukaa' is a stative verb; the state of being seated uses the perfect marker '-me-', hence 'wamekaa'.

quiz.question: Negate the sentence: 'Wanafunzi wameondoka.'
quiz.explanation: The affirmative perfect '-me-' negates directly with the negative subject prefix plus '-ja-' (hawajaondoka).

quiz.question: Translate: 'I have not yet eaten.'
quiz.explanation: 'Si-' (1st person negative) + '-ja-' (not yet) + '-la' (verb stem of kula without ku-) yields 'sijala'.

quiz.question: What does 'Nimechoka' mean?
quiz.explanation: 'Kuchoka' is a stative verb. 'Nimechoka' translates as the present state 'I am tired'.

tip: Whenever you want to say 'not yet' in Swahili, immediately reach for the negative prefix + -ja-! You can pair it with the adverb 'bado'.

title: The Habitual Marker hu- and Infinitive Class Ku-
subtitle: Express timeless truths, daily routines, and actions functioning as nouns
keyPoint: The habitual prefix hu- attaches directly to the verb base without any subject prefix for all persons, while the ku- infinitive functions both as 'to do' and as a verbal noun (Class 15).

examples.en: Yeye husafiri kwa ndege mara nyingi.
Kuvuta sigara kunaharibu afya ya binadamu.
Sisi hula ugali na samaki jioni.

mistakes.note: The habitual marker 'hu-' completely replaces the subject prefix and tense marker; never combine it with personal prefixes like 'ni-'.
Class 15 verbal nouns starting with 'ku-' govern Class 15 concords: 'ku-' and 'kwa-', never Class 1 or 9 forms.
The infinitive verb acting as a complement must retain standard 'ku-': 'kula'.

quiz.question: Fill in the blank with the habitual marker: 'Wakulima ___ mahindi wakati wa masika.' (Farmers usually plant corn...)
quiz.explanation: 'Hupanda' expresses the habitual, timeless routine without personal subject prefixes.

quiz.question: How does Class 15 ('ku-') agree with an adjective? 'Kucheza kule ni ___.'
quiz.explanation: Infinitives belonging to Class 15 take the adjective concord 'ku-', producing 'kuzuri'.

quiz.question: Which sentence correctly uses the habitual aspect?
quiz.explanation: 'Hu-' attaches directly to the stem 'ruka' without any preceding subject marker.

quiz.question: Choose the correct possessive concord for an infinitive: 'Kuandika ___ kumesaidia.' (Your writing has helped)
quiz.explanation: Class 15 nouns require the possessive concord 'kw-', making 'kwako' (your).

tip: The prefix hu- is the easiest verb form in Swahili: whether the subject is 'I', 'you', 'they', or 'elephants', hu- never alters its form or takes subject affixes!

title: Imperatives and the Polite Subjunctive -e
subtitle: Direct commands, plural forms, and polite requests using the final vowel shift
keyPoint: Direct commands use the bare verb stem in the singular and end in -eni in the plural, while polite requests add subject prefixes and change the final vowel to -e.

mistakes.note: Monosyllabic verbs retain the infinitive prefix 'ku-' in the singular imperative.
Polite requests paired with 'tafadhali' require the subjunctive form ending in -e.
'Kwenda' irregular imperative plural commonly uses 'nendeni' or 'endeni', never combining with extra tense prefixes.

quiz.question: How do you politely tell one person: 'Please enter'?
quiz.explanation: The polite request uses the 2nd-person subject prefix 'u-' and changes the final vowel -a to -e.

quiz.question: What is the command telling multiple children to write?
quiz.explanation: Plural commands are formed by dropping the final -a and appending -eni.

quiz.question: Choose the correct hortative for 'Let's drink water':
quiz.explanation: The inclusive hortative 'let us' uses prefix 'tu-' with the subjunctive ending '-e'.

quiz.question: Which form is the correct direct command for the monosyllabic verb 'kuja' (to come)?
quiz.explanation: 'Kuja' is irregular in the imperative singular, taking the special suppletive form 'njoo!'

tip: Whenever you want to sound polite in Swahili, always swap the final -a of the verb to -e and precede it with 'u-' (singular) or 'm-' (plural).

title: Copular Verbs: ni/si, kuwa na, and Locatives
subtitle: Identity with ni/si, possession with -wa na, and location with -ko/-po/-mo
keyPoint: Swahili distinguishes identity (ni/si), possession (subject marker + na), and relative location (subject marker + ko/po/mo).

cells: Is / Are vs Is not / Are not
To have vs Not to have

examples.en: Yeye ni daktari katika hospitali kuu.
Wao si wanafunzi wa shule hii.

mistakes.note: Do not use 'anakuwa' for simple present identity; the invariant copula 'ni' is required.
'Nina' means 'I have'; identity requires 'mimi ni' (I am).
Use '-mo' rather than '-ko' when referencing something specifically inside an enclosed space.

quiz.question: Complete the negative identity: 'Huyu ___ ndugu yangu.' (This is not my brother.)
quiz.explanation: 'Si' is the universal invariant negative copula for identification.

quiz.question: Choose the correct translation for 'They have houses':
quiz.explanation: Possession in the present tense connects the subject prefix 'wa-' directly to 'na' without any copular verb.

quiz.question: Which phrase correctly says 'Where are you (singular)?'
quiz.explanation: 'Uko wapi?' combines the 2nd person singular subject prefix 'u-' with the general locative enclitic '-ko'.

quiz.question: How do you say 'The book is not on the table' (kitabu class 7)?
quiz.explanation: Noun class 7 (ki-) takes negative prefix 'ha-', concord 'ki-', and locative '-ko' yielding 'hakiko'.

tip: Remember: -ko is for general/indefinite location, -po is for a specific pinpoint spot, and -mo is strictly inside a volume or enclosure.

title: The Ji-/Ma- and N- Classes and Concord
subtitle: Navigating consonant shifts, zero-prefixes, and adjective agreements in Classes 5/6 and 9/10
keyPoint: Class 5 often has no visible prefix on the noun but triggers li- prefixes on modifiers, whereas Class 9/10 nouns resist change but alter modifying adjectives through nasal assimilation.

mistakes.note: 'Jina' is in Class 5 (Ji-), so possessives take the 'l-' concord, yielding 'langu', not 'yangu'.
Adjectives modifying Class 9/10 nouns must match N-concord ('nzuri'), never human M/Wa concord ('mzuri').
'Maji' (water) is an uncountable Class 6 (Ma-) noun and requires the demonstrative 'haya'.

quiz.question: Choose the correct demonstrative: 'Daraja ___ limevunjika.' (This bridge has broken - Class 5)
quiz.explanation: 'Daraja' belongs to Class 5, which uses the demonstrative prefix 'li-', resulting in 'hili'.

quiz.question: How do you say 'New books' when using 'vitabu' vs 'New pens' using 'kalamu' (Class 10)?
quiz.explanation: The adjective '-pya' with Class 10 (N- class) takes the nasal consonant prefix 'm-', making 'mpya'.

quiz.question: Select the proper agreement: 'Macho yangu ___uma.' (My eyes hurt)
quiz.explanation: 'Macho' is the plural of 'jicho' (Class 6 Ma-), requiring the verbal subject agreement prefix 'ya-'.

quiz.question: Fill in the blank: 'Simba wawili ___kimbia mwituni.'
quiz.explanation: Although 'simba' morphologically belongs to Class 9/10, all animate beings (humans and animals) govern Class 1/2 verbal concord ('wa-').

tip: Biological animacy always trumps noun morphology: living creatures take Class 1/2 agreement (a-/wa-) even when their noun looks like Class 5 or Class 9.

title: Relative Clauses: amba- vs Synthetic -o-
subtitle: Connecting clauses using separate amba- words or synthetic internal relative infixes
keyPoint: Swahili can express 'who/which/that' either by affixing the -o of reference to the independent base amba-, or by inserting the relative morpheme directly into the verb after the tense marker.

cells: the person who does not read

examples.en: Chakula ambacho kiliandaliwa kilikuwa kitamu sana.

mistakes.wrong: Mtu anasoma ambaye ni kaka yangu.
mistakes.right: Mtu anayesoma ni kaka yangu. / Mtu ambaye anasoma ni kaka yangu.
mistakes.note: 'Amba-' must directly follow the noun it qualifies, or the verb must incorporate the synthetic infix.
Do not repeat unnecessary object markers inside the relative verb unless emphasis or specificity is needed.
Never double the relative marker by using both 'amba-' and the internal -o- infix on the same verb.

quiz.question: Which sentence correctly says 'The food which cooked is sweet' using an infix?
quiz.explanation: Class 7 past relative: ki- (SM) + li (past) + cho (Class 7 relative) + pikwa (root) = kilichopikwa.

quiz.question: Match the correct amba- form for 'nyumba' (Class 10 plural): 'Nyumba ___ zilinunuliwa.'
quiz.explanation: Class 10 noun agreement requires the reference concord '-zo', yielding 'ambazo'.

quiz.question: What is the synthetic negative form of 'Watu wanaokimbia' (People who are running)?
quiz.explanation: Negative relative construction: wa- (SM) + si (negation) + o (Class 2 relative) + kimbia (root) = wasiokimbia.

quiz.question: Which tense marker is NOT permitted when using an internal synthetic relative infix?
quiz.explanation: The perfect tense marker '-me-' cannot host an internal relative infix; one must use 'amba-' instead.

tip: The internal relative infix only works with -na- (present), -li- (past), and -taka- (future). For all other tenses like -me- or conditionals, use 'amba-'!

title: Verbal Extensions: Prepositional and Causative
subtitle: Deriving new verbs with the applicative (-ia/-ea) and causative (-isha/-esha)
keyPoint: Vowel harmony dictates whether extensions use i or e: verbs with root vowels a, i, u select -ia/-isha, while roots containing e or o take -ea/-esha.

mistakes.wrong: Alimsomea barua kwa sababu ya vowel -ia: alisomia.
mistakes.note: Because 'soma' contains the root vowel 'o', the extension vowel must harmony shift to 'e' (-ea), not 'i' (-ia).
Natural Swahili prefers the applicative verb with an object prefix ('-mnunulia') rather than the clunky loan phrase 'kwa ajili ya'.
Rather than using 'fanya' + infinitive to express causation, use the causative form ('liza' from 'lia').

quiz.question: What is the applicative form of 'pika' (to cook)?
quiz.explanation: The root vowel of 'pika' is 'i', so according to vowel harmony, it takes '-ia'.

quiz.question: What is the causative form of 'chemka' (to boil)?
quiz.explanation: The root vowel is 'e', which demands the causative vowel 'e' via harmony: 'chemkesha'.

quiz.question: How do you derive 'to explain / make understand' from 'elewa' (to understand)?
quiz.explanation: 'Eleza' is the standard lexicalized causative extension derived from the stem 'elewa'.

quiz.question: What does 'Aliniandikia barua' mean?
options: He wrote a letter with me.
He made me write a letter.
He wrote a letter for/to me.
He stopped writing me a letter.
quiz.explanation: The applicative extension -ia indicates doing the verbal action for or towards the applied object ('me').

tip: Check the verb's last vowel before the final -a: if it is E or O, use -e- extensions (-ea, -esha). If it is A, I, or U, use -i- extensions (-ia, -isha).

title: Verbal Extensions: Passive and Reciprocal
subtitle: Transforming verbs to show actions received or shared mutually
keyPoint: Add the passive extension -wa to indicate an action done to the subject, and the reciprocal extension -ana to show that multiple subjects perform the action on each other.

examples.en: Sisi hupigiana simu kila mwisho wa juma.

mistakes.note: Use 'na' to introduce the agent of a passive verb, never 'kwa'.
Reciprocal verbs already express mutual action; do not add a direct object pronoun like 'yeye'.
Use 'kwa' for the instrument/tool used, reserving 'na' strictly for the animate agent.

quiz.question: The lost keys were found by Juma: Funguo zilizopotea ___ na Juma.
quiz.explanation: 'Zilipatikana' (or passive 'zilionwa') expresses being found/available, here correctly matching noun class 10.

quiz.question: Amina and Asha help each other: Amina na Asha ___ kila siku.
quiz.explanation: The reciprocal suffix -ana indicates mutual assistance between the two subjects.

quiz.question: This beautiful song was sung by children: Wimbo huu mzuri ___ na watoto.
quiz.explanation: The passive form of 'imba' is 'imbwa' with the agreement prefix 'u-' matching 'wimbo' (Class 3).

quiz.question: We saw each other at the library yesterday: Sisi ___ maktabani jana.
quiz.explanation: 'Tulionana' combines past tense -li- with the reciprocal verb 'onana' (see one another).

tip: Verbs ending in double vowels insert -lewa or -liwa for the passive (e.g., pokea becomes pokelewa, nunua becomes nunuliwa) following standard Swahili vowel harmony.

title: Conditionals: Real, Hypothetical, and Counterfactual
subtitle: Navigating possibilities, present hypotheticals, and past regrets
keyPoint: Use -ki- for real or probable future conditions, -nge- for present hypothetical situations, and -ngali- for past counterfactual events that cannot be changed.

useCases.label: Present Imaginings (-nge-)
useCases.example: Ningekuwa na pesa, ningenunua gari jipya.

examples.en: Ukifanya mazoezi kila siku, utakuwa na afya bora.
Tukiondoka sasa hivi, tutawahi gari la moshi.

mistakes.note: Maintain tense harmony across both clauses; pair -nge- with -nge-, or -ki- with future -ta-.
The negative of conditional -ki- is formed with -sipo-, not -si-ki-.
A counterfactual condition (-ngali-) requires a counterfactual result clause, never future -ta-.

quiz.question: If you study hard, you will pass the exams: ___ kwa bidii, utafaulu mtihani.
quiz.explanation: The real condition leading to a future outcome uses the infix -ki-.

quiz.question: If I had money right now, I would travel: Ningekuwa na pesa, ___ sasa hivi.
quiz.explanation: Present hypothetical conditions pair the protasis -nge- with an apodosis also in -nge-.

quiz.question: If they had arrived yesterday, they would have eaten: Wangalifika jana, ___ chakula kizuri.
quiz.explanation: Past impossible conditions require -ngali- in both the condition and result clauses.

quiz.question: If you do not leave now, you will be late: ___ sasa hivi, utachelewa.
quiz.explanation: The negative conditional for real possibilities is formed using the prefix pattern u-sipo-.

tip: Remember: -ki- looks forward to what may be, -nge- dreams of what could be right now, and -ngali- looks backward at what can never be changed.

title: Stative and Conversive Extensions
subtitle: Expressing intrinsic states, potentiality, and the reversal of actions
keyPoint: The stative extension (-ika/-eka) indicates a state of being or intrinsic potential without an agent, while the conversive extension (-ua/-oa) systematically reverses an action.

examples.en: Kazi hii yote inafanyika haraka sana.
Aliamua kufunua sufuria ili kuangalia nyama.
Saa yangu imeharibika baada ya kuanguka chini.

mistakes.note: Stative verbs (-ika/-eka) cannot take an agent with 'na'; use the passive (-wa) if the agent is mentioned.
To indicate edible quality or ability to be eaten, use the stative extension -lika, not the active verb.
To reverse 'funga' (tie/close), use conversive 'fungua' (untie/open), not applicative 'fungia'.

quiz.question: This water is not drinkable: Maji haya ___ hata kidogo.
quiz.explanation: The stative form of 'nywa' is 'nyweka' (negative: hayanyweki), expressing the intrinsic capability of being drunk.

quiz.question: He unpacked his clothes from the bag: Ali___ nguo zake kutoka kwenye begi.
quiz.explanation: 'Pakua' is the conversive of 'paka' (to load/pack), meaning to unload or unpack.

quiz.question: The glass broke unexpectedly on the floor: Kioo ___ sakafuni ghafla.
quiz.explanation: 'Kilivunjika' denotes an agentless state where an object becomes broken on its own.

quiz.question: Can this task be accomplished today?: Kazi hii ___ leo kweli?
quiz.explanation: The stative 'fanyika' indicates whether the task has the feasibility or potential to get done.

tip: Use vowel harmony: if the root contains vowels A, I, or U, apply -ika / -ua (e.g., vunjika, fungua); if the root has E or O, apply -eka / -oa (e.g., someka, chomoa).

title: Compound Verb Tenses with Auxiliary -kuwa
subtitle: Combining auxiliary and main verbs to convey nuanced aspects
keyPoint: Compound tenses employ an inflected auxiliary form of -kuwa (to be) followed by an inflected main verb to mark precise aspectual combinations like past progressive or future perfect.

useCases.label: Future Projection
useCases.example: Kesho saa nane mchana nitakuwa nikifanya mtihani.

examples.en: Saa tano asubuhi watakuwa wamemaliza kazi zao zote.
Mwizi alikuwa ameshatoroka kabla ya polisi kufika.
Zamani tulikuwa tukienda pwani kila Jumamosi.
Ungalikuja mapema, tungekuwa tunacheza pamoja sasa.

mistakes.note: The main verb in a compound construction must carry full inflection (subject prefix and aspect infix like -na- or -ki-).

mistakes.right: Alikuwa hapendi kula samaki au hakuwa akipenda kula samaki.
mistakes.note: To negate compound tenses, negate either the auxiliary (hakuwa akienda) or keep the auxiliary affirmative with negative main verb.
Ensure the main verb retains its perfective marker -me-, yielding 'tumemaliza', not an uninflected stem.

quiz.question: When father arrived, the children were sleeping: Baba alipofika, watoto ___ kitandani.
quiz.explanation: The past progressive uses auxiliary 'walikuwa' combined with progressive 'wanalala' (or continuous 'wakilala').

quiz.question: By tomorrow morning, we will have arrived in Mombasa: Kufikia kesho asubuhi, ___ Mombasa.
quiz.explanation: The future perfect pairs the future auxiliary 'tutakuwa' with the perfective main verb 'tumefika'.

quiz.question: He had already eaten before the guests arrived: Alikuwa ___ kabla ya wageni kufika.
quiz.explanation: The past perfect (pluperfect) pairs past auxiliary 'alikuwa' with perfective -me- ('amekula').

quiz.question: They were walking to school every day: Walikuwa ___ shuleni kila siku.
quiz.explanation: The participial -ki- tense ('wakienda') expresses habitual or ongoing background action after auxiliary -kuwa.

tip: In the main verb of a compound continuous tense, speakers often prefer the participial infix -ki- (e.g., alikuwa akisoma) over -na- (alikuwa anasoma) to clearly distinguish background duration.

title: Narrative -ka-, Relative -po-, and Concessive Markers
subtitle: Connecting story sequences, temporal moments, and concessive actions
keyPoint: Chain sequential story actions using the narrative infix -ka-, embed time and location using relative -po-, and convey concession ('even if / although') with -japo-.

cells: and then he went to market

useCases.label: Storytelling Sequence (-ka-)
useCases.example: Aliingia ndani, akaketi kitini, akaanza kusoma.

examples.en: Asha aliamka asubuhi na mapema, akapika chai, akaenda kazini.
Tulipomwona mwalimu wetu, tulimsalimu kwa heshima zote.
Ijapokuwa mvua inanyesha kwa wingi, tutasafiri tu.
Mtoto alidondoka chini akalia kwa sauti kuu.
Mahali wanapofanyia kazi ni mbali sana kutoka hapa.

mistakes.wrong: Alikuja jana na alinunua chakula na alikula.
mistakes.note: Avoid repeating past marker -li- in storytelling; establish past once with -li-, then link subsequent actions with -ka-.
Using 'wakati' alongside the relative temporal infix -po- is redundant in standard Swahili syntax.
Do not mix conditional -ki- and concessive -japo- in the same verb stem.

quiz.question: He opened the door and then entered the room: Alifungua mlango, ___ chumbani.
quiz.explanation: The narrative consecutive infix -ka- carries forward the chain of completed events.

quiz.question: When you arrive in Nairobi, call me immediately: ___ Nairobi, nipigie simu mara moja.
quiz.explanation: 'Utakapofika' combines future -ta- with relative temporal -ka-po- to denote 'at the time in the future when you arrive'.

quiz.question: Although he is young, he has great wisdom: ___ mdogo, ana hekima kubwa.
quiz.explanation: The concessive prefix combination 'ajapokuwa' translates to 'although/even if he is'.

quiz.question: The village where they live is very peaceful: Kijiji ___ kina amani tele.
quiz.explanation: The relative infix -po- serves as the general temporal and locative marker matching specific place references.

tip: In rapid storytelling, monosyllabic verb stems retain the infinitive prefix 'ku-' with narrative -ka- (e.g., akala from kula, akaja from kuja).
